issues.description: No regression test added for the state-reuse bug the PR claims to fix
issues.detail: The fix targets two reuse scenarios: (a) the no-op `s.stack = s.stack[0:]` leaving stale stack entries, and (b) no cleanup when `yield` returns false (early termination). The existing tests (TestSort serialized via mutex) only exercise full-iteration reuse, which already left stack at len 0 and therefore didn't reproduce the bug. A test that calls `Sort` twice on the same Sorter where the first iterator is abandoned mid-walk (yield returns false) would lock in the regression. Without it, the next refactor can silently reintroduce the leak.

issues.description: Updated comment contains typos and a grammatical error
issues.detail: Line 83-84: 'visisted' should be 'visited'; 'if its the first' should be 'if it's the first'. The old comment was prose-correct; the rewrite regressed it. Trivial to fix in the same PR.

issues.description: Removal of the `working` constant is correct but undocumented in the commit/PR description
issues.detail: The original `working` state was effectively dead: `push()` checked for `working`, but the loop set `walking` -- wait, the OLD loop actually set `working` (the diff shows `s.state[k] = working` being replaced with `walking`). So `walking` was the dead constant in the old code, and the PR is collapsing the two synonyms into one (`walking`). The change is correct, but the PR description only says 'reduces the internal states' without explaining that `working`/`walking` were duplicates with inconsistent producers/consumers -- which was itself a latent cycle-detection bug (push() looking for `working`, loop setting `working`, matched; but the constant `walking` existed and was checked nowhere). Worth a one-line note in the commit message for future archaeology.

issues.description: `clear(s.stack)` before truncation is correct but only matters for pointer-bearing Node types
issues.detail: `clear(s.stack); s.stack = s.stack[:0]` zeros out backing-array elements so retained Node values (which may be interfaces or pointers) can be GC'd between Sort invocations. For value-typed nodes the clear is wasted work. Not a bug -- the conservative choice is correct since Node is `any`. Worth a brief comment noting intent so a future optimizer doesn't drop the clear.

issues.description: Defer ordering: `iterating = false` runs last, which is intentional but worth verifying for panic-safety
issues.detail: If `dag(node)` or `yield` panics, the defer still clears state and stack and resets `iterating`. Good. However, `clear(s.state)` on a map iterated by user code in a panicking yield is fine since defer runs after the panic unwinds the yield frame. No action required, but I'd add a brief comment that the defer must be panic-safe so the reëntrancy guard isn't permanently latched.

issues.description: Lazy initialization of `s.state` retained but `s.stack` is never lazily initialized
issues.detail: `s.state = make(map[Key]byte)` is created on first call if nil. `s.stack` relies on `append` to allocate, which is fine. The asymmetry is intentional (nil map can't be written to, nil slice can be appended) but worth a one-line comment for readers. Pure nit.

dissents.topic: Should cleanup live in `defer` at the end, or at the start of the next call?

positions.position: Cleaning up in the deferred function guarantees the Sorter is left in a clean state regardless of whether the consumer iterates fully, breaks early, or panics. Future callers don't pay reuse-correctness tax.

Cleaning at the start of the next call defers work until it's actually needed -- if the Sorter is never reused, you save the clear. Also makes post-mortem debugging easier because the final state of the Sorter reflects the last run. The PR's choice is still correct, just a different tradeoff.

dissents.topic: Is moving `s.state[k] = sorted` inside the `if state != sorted` block a behavior change or just a micro-optimization?

positions.position: Old code unconditionally re-wrote `sorted` over `sorted` on the second pop of an already-sorted node. The new code skips the redundant write. Pure efficiency, no semantic change.

If `yield(node)` returns false, the OLD code's `s.state[k] = sorted` was unreachable (early return). The NEW code also doesn't set sorted on early return -- but the defer's `clear(s.state)` wipes everything anyway. Net behavior on early termination is identical; the conditional is purely a cleanup of redundant writes during normal iteration. No semantic regression.

dissents.topic: Is removing `working` a simplification or losing optionality for richer cycle reporting?

positions.position: Two synonymous in-progress states with inconsistent producers/consumers were a latent footgun. Collapsing to one is the right call.

Distinct `working` (children expanded, awaiting completion) vs `walking` (still expanding) states could enable better cycle diagnostics or back-edge classification later. Removing it forecloses that. Counter: YAGNI -- add it back when needed.

review.summary: The PR correctly fixes two real bugs in Sorter reuse: (1) `s.stack = s.stack[0:]` was a no-op that left stale entries when an iterator was abandoned via `yield` returning false, and (2) state was reset at call-start rather than after completion, so an abandoned iterator left the Sorter in a half-walked state that the next caller couldn't observe. Moving cleanup into a `defer` is the right architectural move and makes the Sorter panic-safe. The collapse of `working`/`walking` into a single `walking` constant removes a latent footgun (the two states had inconsistent producer/consumer relationships in the old code). My main concern is the absence of a regression test that actually exercises the early-termination reuse path -- the existing tests would have passed against the broken old code. Comment typos ('visisted', 'if its') should be fixed in the same PR. Recommend merge after adding a reuse-with-early-termination test and fixing the typos.
